contentBlocks.text: Last week you studied colonialism's causes and governance. This week: what happened afterward, its lasting legacies!

Throughout the 20th century, colonized peoples across many regions of the world organized independence movements, seeking self-governance rather than continued rule by a distant colonial power. These movements varied widely in their methods (some primarily political and diplomatic, others involving armed resistance) and timelines, but shared a common goal of ending colonial rule. Using last week's content on why colonial expansion happened, explain why the same reasons a colonial power wanted control over a territory (resources, land, influence) would also be reasons the colonized population wanted that control returned to themselves.
You just learned about the general pattern of 20th-century independence movements! Tomorrow we'll look at a specific challenge many newly independent nations faced: their borders.

objectives: Understand independence movements as a general 20th-century pattern of colonized peoples seeking self-governance
Connect the resources/land/influence motivations from last week to why colonized populations wanted self-governance
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review last week's colonialism-causes-and-governance work briefly.
2. Introduce independence movements as a general worldwide 20th-century pattern.
3. Have the child connect last week's motivations to this week's independence-movement content.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's colonial-borders lesson.
differentiationTips: Struggling: use a simple analogy — if someone took control of your belongings for their own benefit, you would naturally want that control returned to you
Ready for more: ask the child why independence movements might use very different methods (political vs. armed) in different places, even with the same overall goal
Opens this week's colonialism-legacies thread, deliberately continuing at the same general, worldwide level as last week rather than South Asia-specific content
teacherGuide.answerKey: The same resources, land, and influence a colonial power wanted to control were exactly what the colonized population had a direct stake in, since their own land and resources were being controlled by an outside power — so the same underlying value that motivated colonial expansion also motivated the desire for self-governance and independence.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses WA Social Studies and C3 Framework History standards on 20th-century decolonization, opening this week's colonialism-legacies thread as a continuation of last week's unit.
